text: Professional art thieves tend to be surgical. They take the most valuable, most portable pieces and leave the rest. These thieves did the opposite.

text: The list is strange. Five Degas sketches, a Manet, and a Chinese bronze beaker three thousand years old.
provenance: It is a strange, uneven list, and that strangeness is one of the great clues that has never quite been solved.
Alongside the Vermeer and the Rembrandts, the thieves took five works by Degas — small, delicate sketches and watercolors, not the artist's most famous or valuable pieces.
One was an ancient Chinese beaker — a bronze vessel called a Gu, some three thousand years old.

text: The crown of the haul was a Vermeer. Only about three dozen of his works are known to exist anywhere on earth.
provenance: The crown of it was a single painting by Johannes Vermeer

text: None of it can be sold. You cannot walk into an auction house with a cut-out Rembrandt.

Which means their true value is almost philosophical — they are priceless precisely because they can never be sold.

text: Which leaves one uncomfortable answer. Either the thieves did not understand what they were holding, or the art was never really the point. Look again at what they left.
